cards.front: After autophosphorylating its own tyrosines, the insulin receptor phosphorylates the docking protein {{c1::IRS-1}}.
cards.back: Insulin receptor substrate 1.
cards.quote: After autophosphorylating its own tyrosines, the insulin receptor phosphorylates IRS-1 (insulin receptor substrate 1), the docking protein from the adaptors and scaffolds lesson.
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: Which two modules at one end of IRS-1 hold it at the membrane beside the insulin receptor, and what does each bind?
cards.back: A PH domain binds membrane lipids, and a PTB domain binds phosphotyrosine on the activated insulin receptor.
cards.quote: a PH domain (pleckstrin homology domain, which binds membrane lipids) and a PTB domain (phosphotyrosine-binding domain, which binds phosphotyrosine on the receptor).
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: How does phosphorylation of IRS-1's tyrosine-rich tail allow insulin signaling to branch into multiple pathways?
cards.back: Phosphotyrosine motifs on IRS-1 recruit distinct SH2-domain proteins: PI 3-kinase, the adaptor Grb2 (leading to Ras), and the phosphatase Shp2.
cards.quote: recruits proteins carrying SH2 domains (Src homology 2 domains, which recognize specific phosphotyrosine motifs): PI 3-kinase, the adaptor Grb2 (leading to Ras), and the phosphatase Shp2.
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: What two effects does docking PI 3-kinase onto phosphorylated IRS-1 accomplish?
cards.back: It brings PI 3-kinase to its membrane lipid substrate and loosens the regulatory subunit's hold on the catalytic subunit.
cards.why: PI 3-kinase's regulatory subunit uses two SH2 domains to bind phosphotyrosines on IRS-1.
cards.quote: Docking on IRS-1 both brings the enzyme to its membrane substrate and loosens the regulatory subunit's hold on the catalytic one
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: At the plasma membrane, the catalytic subunit of PI 3-kinase adds phosphate to the 3 position of PIP2 to make {{c1::PIP3}}.
cards.back: PI(3,4,5)P3, made from PI(4,5)P2.
cards.quote: which adds phosphate to the 3 position of PIP2 (PI(4,5)P2, phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate) to make PIP3 (PI(3,4,5)P3)
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: Akt (protein kinase B) is a {{c1::serine/threonine}} kinase whose amino-terminal PH domain binds PIP3 at the plasma membrane.
cards.back: Its PH domain also binds the related 3-phosphorylated lipid PI(3,4)P2.
cards.quote: Akt (also called protein kinase B, PKB), a serine/threonine kinase, carries an amino-terminal PH domain that binds PIP3 (and the related 3-phosphorylated lipid PI(3,4)P2)
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: Beyond anchoring Akt at the plasma membrane, what second job does PIP3 binding perform in activating Akt?
cards.back: PIP3 binding opens Akt's folded, self-inhibited shape so PDK1 can reach and phosphorylate Thr308.
cards.quote: Its binding also opens Akt's folded, self-inhibited shape so that PDK1 can reach Thr308
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: Full activation of Akt requires two phosphorylations. Which site does each kinase phosphorylate, and how does each contribute to activity?
cards.back: PDK1 phosphorylates Thr308 in the activation loop (supplying most activity), and mTORC2 phosphorylates Ser473 near the tail (adding to it, for full activity).
cards.why: PDK1 is held at the plasma membrane by its own PH domain.
cards.quote: Akt at the membrane → Thr308-P (PDK1) + Ser473-P (mTORC2) → active Akt
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: Cells lacking mTORC2 activity are treated with insulin while PI 3-kinase, PIP3, and PDK1 remain intact. What happens to Akt activity, and why?
cards.back: Akt gains substantial but sub-maximal activity. PDK1 can still phosphorylate Thr308, which supplies most of Akt's activity, but without Ser473 phosphorylation by mTORC2 it cannot reach full activity.
cards.quote: Thr308 supplies most of the activity, Ser473 adds to it, and both together give full activity
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: You want to engineer a single protein that binds both an activated receptor tyrosine kinase and PIP3 at the plasma membrane. Which two protein modules should you combine?
cards.back: Combine an SH2 domain (or PTB domain) to bind phosphotyrosines on the activated receptor with a PH domain to bind PIP3.
cards.quote: proteins carrying SH2 domains (Src homology 2 domains, which recognize specific phosphotyrosine motifs)
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: Researchers fuse Akt's PIP3-binding (PH) domain to green fluorescent protein (GFP) in insulin-responsive cells. What localization shift happens minutes after insulin arrives, and what does it demonstrate?
cards.back: Fluorescence shifts from the cytosol to the plasma membrane, demonstrating that insulin rapidly drives formation of 3-phosphorylated lipids (such as PIP3) at the plasma membrane.
cards.quote: Fusing Akt's PH domain to green fluorescent protein (GFP) lets you watch those lipids form: minutes after insulin arrives, the glow shifts from the cytosol to the plasma membrane.
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: In cells lacking endogenous Akt, normal Akt is phosphorylated only after insulin, a PH-domain mutant unable to bind PIP3 stays cytosolic and unphosphorylated even with insulin, and an Akt carrying a permanent fatty-acid anchor is membrane-bound and active without insulin. What does this show about PIP3's role?
cards.back: PIP3's first job is recruiting Akt to the plasma membrane, where its activating kinases act; forcing membrane localization bypasses insulin and PIP3, while blocking PIP3 binding prevents activation.
cards.quote: Give Akt a permanent fatty-acid anchor and it sits at the membrane, gains both phosphates and is active with no insulin present.
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: How does requiring both 3-phosphorylated lipids and two phosphorylations restrict Akt activity in space and time?
cards.back: Akt stays strongly active mainly where PI 3-kinase has made 3-phosphorylated lipids downstream of an active receptor, and while those lipids last.
cards.why: Although phosphorylated Akt also reaches cytosolic and nuclear targets, it remains most active while anchored on the lipid.
cards.quote: Together, the lipid and two phosphates keep Akt active mainly where PI 3-kinase has made 3-phosphorylated lipids, downstream of an active receptor, and while those lipids last.
cards.section: Writing the membrane address: from receptor to active Akt

cards.front: {{c1::GLUT4}} is the main insulin-responsive glucose transporter of muscle and fat, stored mostly in intracellular vesicles at rest.
cards.quote: GLUT4 is the main insulin-responsive glucose transporter of muscle and fat, stored mostly in intracellular vesicles at rest.
cards.section: One kinase, three metabolic substrates

cards.front: After 10 minutes of insulin treatment in rat fat cells, glucose transporter counts drop in intracellular membrane fractions and rise by the same amount in plasma membrane fractions, even when protein synthesis is blocked. What mechanism does this demonstrate?
cards.back: Insulin increases surface glucose uptake by moving pre-existing transporters from an internal membrane pool to the plasma membrane rather than synthesizing new transporters.
cards.why: In 1980, Cushman and Wardzala measured this shift by cytochalasin B binding, and Suzuki and Kono confirmed it by reconstituting transport activity into artificial membranes.
cards.quote: Insulin moves transporters from an internal membrane pool to the cell surface.
cards.section: One kinase, three metabolic substrates

cards.front: In a rat fat-cell membrane fractionation assay with protein synthesis blocked, resting cells have 25 units of GLUT4 in the plasma membrane and 75 units in intracellular membranes. If insulin triples surface GLUT4 without changing total transporters, how many units remain intracellular and what percentage of the resting internal pool moved?
cards.back: 25 units remain intracellular, and 66.7% (two-thirds) of the internal pool moved. Setup: total = 25 + 75 = 100 units (conserved). Surface rises to 3 × 25 = 75 units (a 50-unit shift); intracellular falls to 100 − 75 = 25 units; fraction of internal pool moved = 50 / 75 = 66.7%.
cards.quote: Insulin moves transporters from an internal membrane pool to the cell surface.
cards.section: One kinase, three metabolic substrates

cards.front: How does Akt promote fusion of GLUT4 vesicles with the plasma membrane through AS160?
cards.back: Akt phosphorylates and inhibits AS160, a Rab GAP; GLUT4-vesicle Rabs then stay GTP-bound so the vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane.
cards.why: Other insulin-regulated proteins also aid vesicle fusion, and this step was worked out mostly in fat cells.
cards.quote: Akt's phosphate stops AS160 acting on those Rabs, so they stay GTP-bound and the vesicles—helped by other insulin-regulated proteins—fuse with the plasma membrane.
cards.section: One kinase, three metabolic substrates

cards.front: Fat cells express a mutant AS160 that cannot be phosphorylated by Akt but keeps its normal Rab GAP activity. What happens to insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, and why?
cards.back: Insulin-stimulated glucose uptake falls. Because Akt cannot inhibit mutant AS160, it keeps switching GLUT4-vesicle Rab GTPases off, holding GLUT4 vesicles inside the cell.
cards.quote: Akt connects to those vesicles through AS160, a GAP (GTPase-activating protein) for the Rab GTPases directing GLUT4 vesicles.
cards.section: One kinase, three metabolic substrates

cards.front: How does Akt increase glycogen synthesis in muscle and liver via GSK3?
cards.back: Akt phosphorylates and inhibits GSK3, which normally phosphorylates and slows glycogen synthase; phosphatases then strip the inhibitory phosphates from glycogen synthase, speeding it up.
cards.why: Inhibiting GSK3 is one of several ways insulin raises glycogen synthesis.
cards.quote: Akt phosphorylates and inhibits GSK3, letting phosphatases strip the inhibitory phosphates from glycogen synthase—one of several ways insulin raises glycogen synthesis.
cards.section: One kinase, three metabolic substrates

cards.front: A small-molecule drug directly inhibits GSK3 in resting muscle cells with no insulin present. What happens to glycogen synthase phosphorylation and activity, and why?
cards.back: Glycogen synthase loses inhibitory phosphates and speeds up. Blocking GSK3 mimics Akt's inhibition of GSK3, letting cellular phosphatases dephosphorylate and activate glycogen synthase.
cards.quote: Glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) phosphorylates glycogen synthase and keeps it slow.
cards.section: One kinase, three metabolic substrates

cards.front: In the liver between meals, the transcription factor {{c1::FOXO1}} drives expression of gluconeogenic genes including glucose 6-phosphatase and PEP carboxykinase.
cards.quote: FOXO1 is a transcription factor driving gluconeogenic genes—including glucose 6-phosphatase and PEP carboxykinase—between meals.
cards.section: One kinase, three metabolic substrates

cards.front: How does Akt reduce transcription of gluconeogenic genes in the liver through FOXO1?
cards.back: Akt phosphorylates FOXO1, creating binding sites for 14-3-3 proteins that move FOXO1 out of the nucleus and hold it in the cytosol.
cards.quote: Akt phosphorylates FOXO1, the phosphates become binding sites for 14-3-3 proteins, and FOXO1 is moved out of the nucleus and held in the cytosol
cards.section: One kinase, three metabolic substrates

cards.front: Akt exports FOXO1 from the liver nucleus within minutes after a meal. Does that rapid export explain why liver glucose output drops within minutes, and why or why not?
cards.back: No. Although FOXO1 leaves the nucleus within minutes, pre-existing gluconeogenic enzyme proteins take hours to disappear; in mouse experiments the fast drop relies largely on insulin braking adipose fat breakdown.
cards.quote: FOXO1 leaves quickly, but pre-existing enzyme proteins take hours to disappear.
cards.section: One kinase, three metabolic substrates

cards.front: In mouse experiments, insulin still triggers a fast (within-minutes) drop in liver glucose output even without insulin signaling inside liver cells. What does this show, and how does it fit with Akt's control of liver FOXO1?
cards.back: It shows that acute suppression of liver glucose output can rely largely on extrahepatic insulin signaling—braking adipose fat breakdown to lower fatty acids reaching the liver—whereas hepatic Akt–FOXO1 control acts over hours by reducing synthesis of new gluconeogenic enzymes.
cards.why: This combines the lesson's two rules: transcriptional shutoff takes hours because existing enzymes persist, while rapid suppression relies on adipose-to-liver fatty-acid delivery.
cards.quote: work even without insulin signaling in the liver cell, relying largely on insulin braking fat breakdown in adipose tissue to lower fatty acids reaching the liver.
cards.section: One kinase, three metabolic substrates

cards.front: The lipid phosphatase {{c1::PTEN}} helps end PI 3-kinase signaling by erasing PIP3 back to PIP2.
cards.quote: Besides PTEN erasing PIP3 back to PIP2 and tyrosine phosphatases resetting the receptor and IRS-1
cards.section: Ending the signal: erasers and negative feedback

cards.front: Besides PTEN erasing PIP3, which two other classes of phosphatases reset the insulin–Akt pathway, and what does each act on?
cards.back: Tyrosine phosphatases reset the insulin receptor and IRS-1, and protein phosphatases strip Thr308 and Ser473 once Akt leaves the membrane.
cards.quote: tyrosine phosphatases resetting the receptor and IRS-1 (both shown in the second film), protein phosphatases strip Thr308 and Ser473 once Akt leaves the membrane.
cards.section: Ending the signal: erasers and negative feedback

cards.front: How do downstream kinases such as mTORC1 and S6 kinase generate negative feedback on IRS-1?
cards.back: They phosphorylate IRS-1 on serines, making it a poorer substrate for the insulin receptor and potentially marking it for destruction by the proteasome.
cards.why: The effect depends on the site: not every serine site inhibits, and a few support signaling.
cards.quote: Phosphate on these serines makes IRS-1 a poorer receptor substrate and can mark it for destruction by the proteasome.
cards.section: Ending the signal: erasers and negative feedback

cards.front: In a hormone pathway where downstream kinases trigger negative feedback by phosphorylating an upstream docking protein on inhibitory serines, what happens during prolonged hormone exposure if those feedback kinases are blocked?
cards.back: Upstream signaling stays stronger and fades more slowly. Without negative feedback, the docking protein remains a good receptor substrate and can avoid feedback-driven proteasomal destruction.
cards.quote: generate negative feedback (from the signaling circuits lesson: output reduces input so a long signal fades) by phosphorylating IRS-1 on serines.
cards.section: Ending the signal: erasers and negative feedback

cards.front: How does PI 3-kinase recruitment by the PDGF receptor differ from its recruitment by the insulin receptor?
cards.back: The PDGF receptor tyrosine kinase binds PI 3-kinase's regulatory subunit directly on its own phosphotyrosines, with no IRS-1 adaptor in between.
cards.quote: the PDGF receptor binds the regulatory subunit directly on its own phosphotyrosines, with no IRS-1 in between.
cards.section: One pathway, two opposite breaks: cancer and insulin resistance

cards.front: In growth-factor-stimulated cells, how does active Akt promote cell survival and division?
cards.back: Akt inhibits proteins that start programmed cell death and inhibits FOXO transcription factors, which in many cell types drive genes that stop division.
cards.quote: Akt inhibits proteins that start the cell-death programme, and inhibits FOXO again, which in many cell types drives genes that stop division.
cards.section: One pathway, two opposite breaks: cancer and insulin resistance

cards.front: Which two common genetic alterations lock the PI 3-kinase–Akt pathway on in human cancers, and which is an oncogene versus a tumor suppressor?
cards.back: Activating mutations in PIK3CA (an oncogene encoding a PI 3-kinase catalytic subunit) and loss of PTEN (a tumor suppressor).
cards.why: Either break leaves more PIP3 on the plasma membrane and holds more Akt active with less upstream signal.
cards.quote: PIK3CA, encoding a PI 3-kinase catalytic subunit, is among the most often mutated oncogenes in human cancer (including breast, colon and endometrium)
cards.section: One pathway, two opposite breaks: cancer and insulin resistance

cards.front: A tumor cell line has lost both copies of PTEN. Compared with normal cells, what happens to PIP3 and Akt soon after growth factors are removed, and why?
cards.back: PIP3 stays high and Akt stays at the membrane and remains active, whereas normal cells use PTEN to erase PIP3. Without PTEN, PIP3 cannot be erased back to PIP2.
cards.quote: Conversely, many tumours lose the tumour suppressor PTEN. Either way, more PIP3 sits on the membrane and holds more Akt active.
cards.section: One pathway, two opposite breaks: cancer and insulin resistance

cards.front: {{c1::Insulin resistance}} means a given insulin concentration produces less response than it should.
cards.quote: Insulin resistance means a given insulin concentration produces less response than it should.
cards.section: One pathway, two opposite breaks: cancer and insulin resistance

cards.front: How can chronic excess nutrients, lipids, and inflammatory signals drive insulin resistance through IRS-1?
cards.back: They keep serine kinases active, loading IRS-1 with inhibitory phosphoserine so less phosphotyrosine forms, less PI 3-kinase docks, and fewer GLUT4 vesicles reach the surface.
cards.why: How much of human insulin resistance this explains is still argued; some lipid signals act on the receptor itself, and the break is not always at IRS-1.
cards.quote: chronic excess nutrients, lipids and inflammatory signals keep serine kinases active, loading IRS-1 with phosphoserine (some lipid signals act on the receptor itself instead).
cards.section: One pathway, two opposite breaks: cancer and insulin resistance

cards.front: On an insulin dose-response curve (glucose uptake versus insulin), how does losing some receptors when spare receptors remain compare with a post-receptor bottleneck?
cards.back: Losing some receptors shifts the curve right while still approaching the normal maximum at high insulin; a post-receptor bottleneck shifts the curve right and lowers maximal uptake. Saturating remaining spare receptors restores maximal flux, whereas saturating every receptor cannot push past a downstream bottleneck.
cards.quote: With spare receptors present, losing some receptors shifts the curve right—more hormone is needed—yet saturating the remaining receptors approaches the normal maximum.
cards.section: One pathway, two opposite breaks: cancer and insulin resistance

cards.front: How does the pancreas initially compensate for insulin resistance, and when does type 2 diabetes begin?
cards.back: The pancreas compensates by secreting more insulin—often for years—and type 2 diabetes begins when it can no longer compensate.
cards.quote: The pancreas compensates with more insulin—often for years—and type 2 diabetes begins when it no longer can.
cards.section: One pathway, two opposite breaks: cancer and insulin resistance

cards.front: Cells responsive to both insulin and PDGF are pre-treated with compound X. Insulin-receptor autophosphorylation is unchanged, IRS-1 carries more phosphoserine, less PI 3-kinase is pulled down with IRS-1, and insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation drops by half, while PDGF-stimulated Akt phosphorylation is unchanged. Which step is impaired, and what rule proves downstream steps are intact?
cards.back: Compound X impairs IRS-1 tyrosine phosphorylation (and PI 3-kinase docking on IRS-1). Because the PDGF receptor binds PI 3-kinase directly without IRS-1, intact PDGF-driven Akt phosphorylation proves PI 3-kinase, PIP3 synthesis, and Akt activation are undamaged.
cards.quote: the PDGF receptor binds the regulatory subunit directly on its own phosphotyrosines, with no IRS-1 in between.
cards.section: One pathway, two opposite breaks: cancer and insulin resistance

cards.front: Muscle cells have insulin resistance caused by heavy inhibitory serine phosphorylation on IRS-1. If you express an Akt variant carrying a permanent fatty-acid membrane anchor in these cells, what happens to surface GLUT4 and glycogen synthesis even without added insulin, and which two pathway rules explain it?
cards.back: Both surface GLUT4 and glycogen synthesis would be expected to rise. First, a permanent fatty-acid anchor puts Akt at the membrane where it gains both activating phosphates without insulin, bypassing the upstream IRS-1 block; second, active Akt releases the brakes on GLUT4 vesicle fusion and glycogen synthase.
cards.quote: less phosphotyrosine appears on IRS-1, less PI 3-kinase docks, and fewer GLUT4 vesicles reach the surface.
cards.section: One pathway, two opposite breaks: cancer and insulin resistance

cards.front: Across glucose uptake (AS160), glycogen storage (GSK3), and liver gluconeogenic gene transcription (FOXO1), what common regulatory sign does Akt apply to all three substrates, and how does that yield opposite metabolic outcomes?
cards.back: Akt switches all three substrates off. Turning off AS160 and GSK3 releases brakes on GLUT4 fusion and glycogen synthesis (activating uptake and storage), whereas turning off FOXO1 removes a transcriptional activator of gluconeogenic genes (suppressing glucose production).
cards.why: This applies the lesson's rule that in its main metabolic examples, Akt's phosphorylation inhibits its substrates.
cards.quote: In every case Akt turns its substrate off—releasing brakes on glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis, and shutting off a transcriptional activator of glucose production.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A person inherits one faulty copy of AKT2 (the main Akt gene in muscle and liver) with a kinase-domain mutation that interferes with the normal Akt protein. Why is the defect worse than a 50% drop in Akt, and what happens to post-meal glucose uptake, glycogen storage, liver glucose output, and insulin levels?
cards.back: Because the mutant kinase blocks the normal copy, functional Akt activity falls well below half. Post-meal GLUT4 translocation weakens, glycogen storage slows, the liver keeps making glucose despite insulin, blood glucose rises, and the pancreas secretes more insulin.
cards.why: This rests on the rule that muscle and liver rely on AKT2 across all three metabolic jobs, so an interfering single-copy mutation produces severe insulin resistance and diabetes.
cards.quote: With one faulty copy you might expect half the Akt and a mild defect. Predict a larger one if the faulty protein also interferes with the normal one.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why did the first pancreatic extract given to Leonard Thompson in January 1922 fail clinically, and what purification strategy did James Collip use to solve it?
cards.back: It was too impure, causing an abscess with little blood-sugar drop; Collip raised alcohol in steps to precipitate impurities first, then precipitated and collected the active insulin.
cards.quote: raised the alcohol concentration of the extract in steps so that impurities dropped out of solution while the active substance stayed in
cards.section: The hormone before the pathway: Toronto, 1921 to 1922

cards.front: What is the "insulin-resistant liver" paradox, and what two competing explanations are debated to account for it?
cards.back: The insulin-resistant liver fails to shut off glucose production yet continues making fat. Researchers debate whether hepatic insulin signaling (potentially involving mTORC1) still drives fat synthesis, or whether excess supply of nutrients and fatty acids drives it.
cards.why: This rests on the lesson's observation that gluconeogenic suppression fails while lipogenesis persists, suggesting either a spared signaling branch or substrate-driven fat synthesis.
cards.quote: There is also a puzzle: the insulin-resistant liver fails to shut off glucose production, yet goes on making fat.
cards.section: Insulin-resistant liver: a puzzle
